newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope in Poland tries to allay health concerns.
newsitem.headline: Pope in Poland tries to allay health concerns.

text.p: Pope John Paul has sought to allay concerns about his health, joking about his age and making an unscheduled foray on foot to greet wellwishers during a strenuous tour of his home country of Poland.

The Pope, who is believed to suffer from Parkinson's disease, broke with his official programme when he left Wroclaw cathedral at the end of a busy official day on Sunday and walked 200 metres (yards) among supporters.

He had looked tired earlier at the start of the first large open air mass of his 11-day visit, but he showed much of his old vigour when he delivered a strong homily in defence of the Roman Catholic Church as a guardian of freedom.
The crowd of 200,000 worshippers roared in appreciation when he told them: "See, I'm still alive. I just turned 77."
Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said the Pope was "very well...One can see that he is happy to be home."
Despite the concerns about his age and health, the Pope has set himself a punishing schedule of visits to 12 cities during the seventh return of his pontificate to Poland.
He will go to Legnica in southwest Poland on Monday to celebrate mass at an airfield which was a main Soviet military base when the country was under communist rule.
The Catholic Church's popular support has slumped in Poland since the 1980s when, along with the Solidarity free trade union, it was in the forefront of the country's struggle for democracy.

The Pope's visit coincides with the start of an election campaign in which the current government led by ex-communists turned social democrats is under challenge from a pro-church coalition mustered by Solidarity.

Without intervening directly in the political battle, the Pope has sought to uphold the church's moral values at a time when rapid economic and social change in Poland has created losers as well as winners.
In his Wroclaw homily, he warned of the dangers of a society "permeated by ideas of democracy inspired by liberal ideology."
He rejected the claims of critics seeking a more secular society that the church was an obstacle to progress.
"Saying that the church is an enemy of freedom makes no sense, especially here in Poland," he said. "The church has proved many times in the last 50 years that it is the guardian of freedom."
